docs.title: Cue
docs.text:
Per-person attention budgets for AI agents and background automations, self-hosted.

A code-review agent, a log-triage agent and a billing agent can all page the same engineer at 2 a.m. A LangGraph interrupt() or a Slack approve button pauses one agent; none of them knows what the others already sent. Cue sits in front of all of them as the outbound gatekeeper:

  • Budgets per agent, per person. Each agent sends with its own key. Its frequency_caps limit how many messages it may send one person per period, and messages over budget are stored as suppressed with reason agent_budget. Category caps count what a person gets from every sender together. See agents.
  • Quiet hours in the person's time zone. A message due inside someone's quiet hours waits until they end. Only critical messages in categories people cannot unsubscribe from break through, and each agent's max_importance caps what it may claim, so only agents you trust can use critical. See delivery policy.
  • Digests for the rest. A digest rule turns a stream of agent events into one message per window, or one per day at a local time.
  • Approval for risky messages. Messages that match an agent's approval condition wait as pending_approval; a reviewer decides from a one-time link in their own notification. Agent keys can never approve. See approval.
  • A reason for every outcome. Each message has a status and a status_reason, and each event records which rules matched and why. Agents connect over HTTP, the SDKs or the MCP server.

The recording is examples/agents-demo: from a checkout, uv run python examples/agents-demo/demo.py runs it with SQLite and the console connector.

docs.title: Your own product's notifications
docs.text:
The same policy serves your product's notifications. Your product and your agents report what happened; Cue decides whether it is worth a notification, what to say, when and over which route, renders a ready-to-send message, and hands it to the delivery you plug in: your own service through a signed webhook, or a ready-made connector.

flowchart LR
    A[Your backend] -- "POST /v1/events" --> B[Rules]
    B --> C[Policy<br/>preferences · caps · quiet hours]
    C --> D[Templates<br/>+ optional AI]
    D --> E{Your delivery}
    E --> F[Webhook → your service]
    E --> G[Connectors<br/>FCM · APNs · Twilio · SMTP · SES · Resend · Slack · Telegram]
    E --> H[Your own plugin]

docs.title: Why Cue?
docs.text:
Most products start with send_push(user, "Your order shipped") sprinkled through the codebase. It works until it doesn't: people get five notifications at 3 a.m., marketing ignores unsubscribes, one dead device token fails a whole job, and nobody can answer "why didn't this user get the message?".

Cue moves that logic into one place:

  • Events, not sends. Your code emits facts (order.shipped); rules decide what to send. Change messaging without redeploying your product.
  • Policy everywhere. Every message — rule-triggered, direct or broadcast — passes the same checks: unsubscribes, muted channels, frequency caps, cooldowns and quiet hours in the recipient's own time zone.
  • Fewer, better messages. Digests turn a burst of events into one message ("Ann, Bo and 10 others commented"), automatically or summarised by AI, and thread ids let phones and inboxes stack related messages.
  • People in control. A preference centre, hosted or headless, one-click unsubscribe as Gmail and Yahoo require, and a consent ledger recording who changed what, and when.
  • Bring your own delivery. Cue does not lock you into a provider. Point a route at your existing sending service with a signed webhook, use a bundled connector, or write your own in a few dozen lines.
  • Reliable routing. Multiple devices per person, channel fallback (push → SMS), retries with backoff, automatic removal of dead tokens, at-least-once jobs that are safe to retry.
  • Answers, not guesses. Every event records which rules matched and why; every message records its status and the reason it was suppressed or failed.
  • AI that cannot lie about money. Optional personalisation through any major model provider, constrained to rephrasing: numbers and links must survive verbatim, and only attributes you allow-list are ever sent to the model.
  • Agent-ready. An MCP server lets AI agents send notifications and inspect delivery with scoped credentials.
  • Runs on your database. An API process and a worker process (or the worker embedded in the API) with PostgreSQL or SQLite. No Redis or message broker: the job queue lives in the database. Retention (cuectl prune) is a command you schedule.

docs.title: Design decisions
docs.text:
The database is the queue. Jobs are rows written in the same transaction as the data they act on (transactional outbox), so there is no window where an event exists without its processing job or a message without its delivery. Delays and quiet hours are a future run_at, which survives restarts without a separate scheduler. Retention is the exception: cuectl prune runs only when you schedule it. Workers claim with SELECT … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED and a conditional update that doubles as a lease; crashed workers' jobs reappear when the lease expires. This removes Redis and a broker from the deployment at the cost of throughput: on the modest 4-vCPU machine in the performance guide, Cue decided and delivered 56 events per second with one worker process and 164 with four. Measure on your own hardware with the bundled benchmark.

One composer. Rules, direct sends and broadcasts all build an intent and pass it to services.composer. Policy cannot be bypassed by adding a new way to send.

Policy is serialised per recipient. Composing locks the recipient row, so caps and cooldowns are exact under concurrency. On SQLite, BEGIN IMMEDIATE provides the same guarantee by serialising writers.

Decisions are data. Suppressed and failed messages are stored with reasons; events store per-rule outcomes. Debugging is a query, not a log search.

Render early, personalise late. Templates render when the message is composed (so errors surface immediately and content is auditable); AI personalisation runs at send time, after policy, so tokens are never spent on messages that will not be sent.

Idempotency everywhere. Events dedupe on (source, idempotency_key) (an agent key's source is always agent:<key>, so it cannot claim another producer's keys); messages on dedup_key (event:<id>:<rule>, broadcast:<id>:<recipient>, api:<key>:<key>); jobs on key. Every job handler re-checks state before acting, so at-least-once execution is safe.

UUIDv7 keys. Time-ordered identifiers keep indexes compact and double as stable pagination cursors.

Plugins over configuration flags. Channels are classes discovered through entry points, configured by name. Adding a provider never touches the core.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text: This walk-through runs Cue locally, sends a notification through a rule, shows it arriving, and shows how to see what happened. The console channel logs messages instead of sending them, so no third-party accounts are needed.

docs.title: 1. Run Cue
docs.text:
Docker ComposePythonuvx

PostgreSQL, a migration job, the API and a separate worker:

git clone https://github.com/murtazox04/Cue && cd Cue
docker compose up --build -d
docker compose exec api cuectl keys create admin

Messages are delivered by the worker service. Follow its log in a second terminal; the notification from step 4 appears there:

docker compose logs -f worker

Python 3.12 or newer, SQLite in ./cue.db, and the worker running inside the API process. Install into a virtual environment:

python -m venv .venv && . .venv/bin/activate
pip install cue-notify

or as a tool with uv: uv tool install cue-notify. Then, in the directory where cue.db should live:

export CUE_WORKER__EMBEDDED=true
export CUE_CHANNELS__PUSH__PROVIDER=console CUE_CHANNELS__SMS__PROVIDER=console
cuectl db upgrade
cuectl keys create admin
cuectl serve

cuectl serve listens on 127.0.0.1:8000 and runs jobs in the same process; the notification from step 4 appears in its output. Run the curl commands below in a second terminal.

Nothing to install besides uv:

CUE_WORKER__EMBEDDED=true CUE_CHANNELS__PUSH__PROVIDER=console \
  CUE_CHANNELS__SMS__PROVIDER=console uvx cue-notify serve --migrate

In a second terminal, in the same directory (both commands use ./cue.db):

uvx cue-notify keys create admin

keys create prints an API key once. Keep it in your shell:

export CUE_API_KEY=ck_…

Interactive API docs are now at http://localhost:8000/docs.

docs.title: 2. Create a template
docs.text:
Templates are Jinja2. data holds the event payload, recipient the person's profile and event the event itself; see templates for the rest.

curl -X POST localhost:8000/v1/templates \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $CUE_API_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "key": "order-shipped",
    "default_locale": "en",
    "locales": {
      "en": {
        "title": "Your order is on its way",
        "body": "Order {{ data.order_id }} ships with {{ data.carrier }}.",
        "url": "https://shop.example/orders/{{ data.order_id }}",
        "channels": {"sms": {"body": "Order {{ data.order_id }} shipped."}}
      },
      "uz": {
        "title": "Buyurtmangiz yo‘lda",
        "body": "{{ data.order_id }} buyurtmangiz {{ data.carrier }} orqali jo‘natildi."
      }
    }
  }'

docs.title: 3. Create a rule
docs.text:
A rule says when this event happens (and this condition holds), send this template on these channels.

curl -X POST localhost:8000/v1/rules \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $CUE_API_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "key": "notify-order-shipped",
    "name": "Tell customers their order shipped",
    "event": "order.shipped",
    "template": "order-shipped",
    "category": "transactional",
    "channels": ["push", "sms"]
  }'

channels is a fallback order: push first, SMS if push is impossible or fails permanently.

docs.title: 4. Send an event
docs.text:
Your backend reports what happened. The recipient can be referenced by id or created inline, with their devices:

curl -X POST localhost:8000/v1/events \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $CUE_API_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "name": "order.shipped",
    "idempotency_key": "order-1001-shipped",
    "recipient": {
      "external_id": "customer-42",
      "locale": "uz",
      "timezone": "Asia/Tashkent",
      "addresses": [{"channel": "push", "value": "device-token-abc"}]
    },
    "data": {"order_id": "1001", "carrier": "UzPost"}
  }'

The response is 202 Accepted; processing happens in the background. About a second later the console channel prints the notification in the worker's log (docker compose logs -f worker, or the terminal running cuectl serve):

INFO    cue_notify.channels.console: [push → device-token-abc] Buyurtmangiz yo‘lda — 1001 buyurtmangiz UzPost orqali jo‘natildi. message_id=…
INFO    cue_notify.services.delivery: message sent message_id=… channel=push

The message is in Uzbek because the recipient's locale is uz. The transactional category ignores quiet hours, so it goes out at once whatever the time in Tashkent.

Retrying the same request returns 200 with "duplicate": true and sends nothing; always set idempotency_key in production. Inline addresses need the recipients:write scope, which the admin key has; see events.

docs.title: 5. See what happened
docs.text:
curl "localhost:8000/v1/events/<event id>" -H "Authorization: Bearer $CUE_API_KEY"
curl "localhost:8000/v1/messages?recipient=customer-42" -H "Authorization: Bearer $CUE_API_KEY"

The event's outcome lists every rule that was considered and why it did or did not fire. Each message shows its status (queued, sending, sent, delivered, failed, suppressed, cancelled, pending_approval) and a status_reason; every value is explained in statuses and reasons. Only queued messages can be cancelled; once a worker claims one it is sending.

To test a rule change without sending anything:

curl -X POST localhost:8000/v1/rules/evaluate \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $CUE_API_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"name": "order.shipped", "recipient": "customer-42", "data": {"order_id": "1", "carrier": "X"}}'

docs.title: 6. Optional: deliver to your own service
docs.text:
Swap the console for the webhook connector to see what your sending service would receive. Save this receiver as receiver.py; it checks the signature and prints the message:

import hashlib
import hmac
import os
from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, HTTPServer

SECRET = os.environ["CUE_CHANNELS__PUSH__SECRET"].encode()


class Receiver(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def do_POST(self):
        body = self.rfile.read(int(self.headers["Content-Length"]))
        signature = dict(part.split("=", 1) for part in self.headers["Cue-Signature"].split(","))
        signed = f"{signature['t']}.".encode() + body
        expected = hmac.new(SECRET, signed, hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()
        print("Cue-Signature:", self.headers["Cue-Signature"])
        print("valid:", hmac.compare_digest(expected, signature["v1"]))
        print(body.decode(), flush=True)
        self.send_response(204)
        self.end_headers()


HTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", 9100), Receiver).serve_forever()

Stop cuectl serve, then pick a secret, start the receiver and start Cue again with the push route pointing at it (Python path shown; with Compose, put the variables in .env and use an address the worker container can reach):

export CUE_CHANNELS__PUSH__SECRET=$(python -c 'import secrets; print(secrets.token_urlsafe(32))')
python receiver.py &
export CUE_CHANNELS__PUSH__PROVIDER=webhook CUE_CHANNELS__PUSH__URL=http://127.0.0.1:9100/push
cuectl serve

Send the event from step 4 again with a new idempotency_key. The receiver prints:

Cue-Signature: t=1791773920,v1=3717d6a9…
valid: True
{"id":"01a12e0c-…","channel":"push","address":"device-token-abc","locale":"uz","importance":"normal","expires_at":null,"content":{"title":"Buyurtmangiz yo‘lda","body":"1001 buyurtmangiz UzPost orqali jo‘natildi.","data":{},"actions":[]},"metadata":{"cue_message_id":"01a12e0c-…","cue_tracking_token":"…"},"links":{}}

In production, verify with the SDKs' verify_webhook / verifyWebhook, which also reject old timestamps, and deduplicate on the Idempotency-Key header. The payload and signature are described in channels.
