docs.title: Events and a rule
docs.text:
Each hook becomes an event named after it: agent.stop, agent.notification, agent.session_end. Their data holds hook, session_id, project, agent, and, when the agent sends them, message and stop_reason.

POST /v1/rules
{"key": "agents-waiting", "name": "Agent needs me", "event": "agent.notification",
 "template": "agent-waiting", "category": "agents", "channels": ["push", "telegram"],
 "importance": "high", "digest": {"window": "PT2M", "send_after": 5}}

The digest turns five agents stopping within two minutes into one notification. Create the agents category first (POST /v1/categories), with whatever caps suit you.

The hook never blocks the agent. It always exits 0 and writes failures to stderr.

docs.title: Compliance
docs.text: Cue keeps a few legal safety nets for messages that need consent: legal hours and caps for marketing texts in the US, opt-out replies, and a consent ledger that records how each change was made. They are guard rails, not legal advice; check what applies to you.

docs.title: Marketing categories
docs.text:
Mark the categories that carry promotions:

POST /v1/categories  {"key": "deals", "marketing": true, "allow_unsubscribe": true}

The built-in marketing category is marked already. Receipts, codes and alerts belong in categories that are not marketing.

docs.title: US texting hours and caps
docs.text:
[compliance]
us_texting_rules = true
sms_channels = ["sms"]   # your channels that send text messages
unknown_state = "strict" # or "federal"

When it is on, a marketing message planned for a text channel and a US recipient is held until the recipient's legal hours, in their time zone. The hours are checked again right before sending, so a retry or a late approval cannot send outside them. In states with a cap, a fourth marketing message within 24 hours is suppressed with status_reason: "compliance: 3 marketing texts per 24 hours (…)". Transactional texts and other channels are not affected.

Jurisdiction Hours (recipient's local time) Cap per 24 h Source US (federal) 8:00–21:00 — 47 CFR 64.1200(c)(1) Connecticut 9:00–20:00 — Conn. Gen. Stat. 42-288a(c) Florida 8:00–20:00 3 Fla. Stat. 501.616(6) Maryland 8:00–20:00 3 Md. Code, Com. Law 14-4502(c) Oklahoma 8:00–20:00 3 Okla. Stat. tit. 15, 775C.4 Oregon 8:00–20:00 3 Oregon HB 3865 (2025) Texas 9:00–21:00; Sundays 12:00–21:00 — Tex. Bus. & Com. Code 301.051(b)(2) Utah 8:00–21:00; not on Sundays — Utah Code 13-25a-103(3) Virginia 8:00–21:00 — Va. Code 59.1-511 Washington 8:00–20:00 — RCW 80.36.390(8) Strict (state unknown) 9:00–20:00, not on Sundays 3 all of the above

How Cue knows where someone is. Set the recipient's region (ISO 3166: US, US-FL) and timezone. Without a region, a +1 number counts as a US recipient in an unknown state, and unknown_state decides between the strict window (the default) and the federal one. The table reflects statutes checked in October 2026. Some state rules are written for calls, and whether they reach texts is unsettled; Cue applies them to texts to stay on the safe side. Legal holidays (Utah, among others) are not modelled; add them with quiet hours if you need them.

docs.title: STOP and START replies
docs.text:
The FCC treats a reply of stop, quit, end, revoke, opt out, cancel or unsubscribe as withdrawn consent, to be honoured within 10 business days (47 CFR 64.1200(a)(10)). Cue honours it at once. For every recipient with that number:

  • On STOP: text messages are muted, and the person is unsubscribed from every optional category.
  • On START (or UNSTOP, YES): text messages come back. Categories stay unsubscribed until the person opts in again.
  • Recorded: both changes go into the consent ledger with source sms_keyword, the keyword and the number.

Report replies from any provider:

POST /v1/inbound/sms  {"from": "+15551230000", "body": "STOP", "message_id": "SM…"}

Or point Twilio's incoming-message webhook at https://<api.public_url>/v1/inbound/twilio. Cue checks Twilio's request signature with the auth token of the Twilio channel listed in sms_channels. Twilio's own opt-out handling still replies to the person; Cue makes sure nothing more is planned for them.

FCC 26-67

On 30 September 2026 the FCC adopted an order that replaces the "revoke-all" rule due on 31 January 2027. Once it takes effect, opting out of informational messages may be limited to the category the person named. Marketing opt-outs still stop all marketing, and the standard keywords must still be honoured. Cue's STOP handling already does the stricter of the two, which satisfies both.

docs.title: Consent ledger and provenance
docs.text:
Every change to someone's preferences is kept (GET /v1/recipients/{id}/preferences/history) with who (source), what (changes), when (created_at) and how (provenance):

Source Provenance Hosted page and preference API method, ip, user_agent One-click unsubscribe method: "one_click", ip, user_agent STOP / START method: "sms_reply", keyword, from, message_id, provider or api_key Your backend method: "api", api_key

docs.title: Recording opt-ins
docs.text:
Regulators expect you to show who agreed, when, how, and to what. Record each opt-in with the exact wording the person saw:

POST /v1/recipients/{id}/consent
{
  "categories": ["marketing"],
  "disclosure": "Yes, text me deals from Shop. Msg & data rates may apply. Reply STOP to end.",
  "disclosure_version": "2026-10",
  "method": "checkbox",
  "source": "https://shop.example/checkout",
  "ip": "198.51.100.7",
  "user_agent": "Mozilla/5.0 …",
  "expires_at": "2027-10-11T00:00:00Z"
}

Cue subscribes the person to those categories. It writes a ledger entry with the disclosure text, its SHA-256, the method, the source, the IP address, the user agent and the time. The entry is written even if the person was already subscribed.

With expires_at, messages in those categories are suppressed with status_reason: "consent_expired" after that moment, until consent is recorded again. France, for example, limits consent to telephone canvassing to one year. Agent keys cannot record consent.

docs.title: Custom channels
docs.text:
A channel provider is a class with a config model and one send method. Package it and register it under the cue.channels entry point; Cue discovers it at start-up.

# my_cue_whatsapp/channel.py
from typing import ClassVar

import httpx
from pydantic import SecretStr

from cue_notify.channels import (
    Channel,
    ChannelConfig,
    Delivery,
    InvalidAddressError,
    Receipt,
    raise_for_http,
    transport_error,
)


class WhatsAppConfig(ChannelConfig):
    phone_number_id: str
    access_token: SecretStr


class WhatsAppChannel(Channel[WhatsAppConfig]):
    provider: ClassVar[str] = "whatsapp"
    config_model: ClassVar[type[ChannelConfig]] = WhatsAppConfig

    async def send(self, delivery: Delivery) -> Receipt:
        try:
            response = await self.http.post(
                f"https://graph.facebook.com/v21.0/{self.config.phone_number_id}/messages",
                headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {self.config.access_token.get_secret_value()}"},
                json={
                    "messaging_product": "whatsapp",
                    "to": delivery.address,
                    "type": "text",
                    "text": {"body": delivery.content.body},
                },
            )
        except httpx.HTTPError as exc:
            raise transport_error(exc) from exc  # network trouble: retryable
        if response.status_code == 400 and "recipient" in response.text:
            raise InvalidAddressError(response.text)
        raise_for_http(response)  # 429/5xx → retryable, other errors → permanent
        return Receipt(provider_message_id=response.json()["messages"][0]["id"])

# your package's pyproject.toml
[project.entry-points."cue.channels"]
whatsapp = "my_cue_whatsapp.channel:WhatsAppChannel"

# cue.toml
[channels.whatsapp]
provider = "whatsapp"
phone_number_id = "1234567890"

docs.title: The contract
docs.text:
• send handles one address. Cue fans out over a recipient's addresses and channels, retries and records results.
  • Use the shared self.http client (connection pooling, sane timeouts).
  • Classify failures (raise_for_http and transport_error cover the common HTTP cases):
    • InvalidAddressError — the address will never work; it gets disabled.
    • DeliveryError(retryable=True, retry_after=…) — transient; the job is retried.
    • DeliveryError(retryable=False) — permanent for this message; the next channel is tried.
  • Return a Receipt with the provider's message id when there is one.
  • delivery.metadata carries cue_message_id and cue_tracking_token; include them in the payload if your channel can carry data to a client app.
  • delivery.links carries preferences and unsubscribe URLs when configured; an e-mail connector should turn unsubscribe into List-Unsubscribe headers.
  • Override aclose() if you hold resources other than the shared HTTP client.

Test providers with httpx.MockTransport — see tests/unit/test_channels.py.

docs.title: Deployment
docs.text: Cue is two processes from one image — the API (cuectl serve) and the worker (cuectl worker) — and a database. Scale both horizontally.

docs.title: Container image
docs.text:
docker build -t cue .                               # everything, including AI
docker build -t cue --build-arg EXTRAS="postgres fcm metrics" .   # without AI

Released images are published as ghcr.io/murtazox04/cue:<version> (for example 0.4.0) and ghcr.io/murtazox04/cue:<major>.<minor> (for example 0.4, which follows patch releases). The versions are listed on the releases page; pin an exact version in production.

The image's entrypoint is cuectl and its default command is serve --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000. It runs as an unprivileged user, contains no source tree, logs JSON and has a health check on /healthz. compose.yaml is a complete reference stack.

docs.title: Production checklist
docs.text:
• PostgreSQL. SQLite serialises all writes and suits single-process installs only. Use postgresql+asyncpg://… and size database.pool_size × processes below the server's max_connections.
  • Migrations before rollout. Run cuectl db upgrade as a one-off job/init container before starting new versions.
  • Separate workers for anything beyond small installs; keep worker.embedded=false. Workers coordinate through the database (FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED), so any number can run. worker.concurrency is per process.
  • Graceful shutdown. Workers finish in-flight jobs on SIGTERM within worker.shutdown_timeout; set your orchestrator's grace period higher.
  • Probes. Liveness: GET /healthz. Readiness: GET /readyz (checks the database).
  • Metrics. Set metrics = true and scrape /metrics (install the metrics extra). /metrics has no key; keep it off the public ingress (the Helm chart routes it only inside the cluster).
  • TLS and network. Terminate TLS at your ingress. Without a key, only the probes, /v1/track/*, and the token pages (/preferences/…, /review/…, Twilio's webhook) are reachable.
  • Request size. Bodies over api.max_body_bytes (1 MiB) are refused with 413 before they are read. Only POST /v1/broadcasts with an admin key may send up to api.max_broadcast_body_bytes. Set a similar limit at your proxy as well.
  • Rate limits. The routes reachable without a key (/preferences/…, /review/…, /v1/track/…, /v1/inbound/…) are limited per client address, and so are failed logins: after too many 401s on /v1, requests from that address without a valid key get 429 for a while (valid keys keep working). See api.rate_limit. Behind a proxy, list it in api.trusted_proxies, or every client shares the proxy's address. The limits are kept in each process: with several replicas or --workers, a client gets the limit once per process. Add a limit at your reverse proxy or ingress as well for multi-replica setups.
  • Bind address. cuectl serve listens on 127.0.0.1 unless you pass --host 0.0.0.0; the image, Compose file, Helm chart and Render Blueprint pass it.
  • HTTPS links. Set api.public_url to an https:// URL. A plain-http URL (other than localhost) logs a warning at startup and fails cuectl check.
  • Secret key. api.public_url requires api.secret_key (CUE_API__SECRET_KEY), which signs preference and unsubscribe links. Generate it once: python -c 'import secrets; print(secrets.token_urlsafe(32))' (at least 32 characters), keep it in your secret store, and give the same value to every API and worker process: a link signed by a worker must verify on the API. Changing it later breaks every preference and unsubscribe link already sent, so rotate it only if it leaks. The Render Blueprint generates one for you.
  • Check before rollout. cuectl check validates the configuration and the database connection and exits with status 1 when it finds an unsafe setting (an unsigned webhook, a plain-http public URL), listing it under warnings.
  • Logs. Tokens in paths (preference pages, review links, open tracking) are replaced with [redacted] in Cue's logs. Your proxy's access log is yours to redact.
  • Retention. Nothing is deleted unless you run cuectl prune; the worker does not run it for you. Schedule it daily with the same configuration as the API, for example from cron (0 3 * * * cuectl prune --older-than 90) or a Kubernetes CronJob running the image with the arguments prune --older-than 90. It deletes in batches of --batch-size rows (1000), each in its own transaction, so it can run while Cue is serving. The consent ledger is proof of consent, so it is kept unless you add --ledger-older-than DAYS.
  • Dead jobs. cuectl jobs stats shows jobs that exhausted retries; cuectl jobs retry-dead requeues them after you fix the cause, and reopens the events, messages, broadcasts and digests they had marked failed.

docs.title: Delivery guarantees
docs.text: Jobs are at least once. Every handler is idempotent with respect to Cue's own state, but if a worker dies after a provider accepted a message and before recording it, the message can be sent again. Webhook deliveries carry an Idempotency-Key header so receivers can deduplicate.

docs.title: Kubernetes (Helm)
docs.text:
The chart in deploy/helm/cue runs the API and the worker against your PostgreSQL:

kubectl create secret generic cue-secrets \
  --from-literal=secret-key="$(python -c 'import secrets; print(secrets.token_urlsafe(32))')"
helm install cue ./deploy/helm/cue \
  --set database.existingSecret=cue-db \
  --set env.CUE_API__PUBLIC_URL=https://cue.example.com \
  --set secretEnv.CUE_API__SECRET_KEY.secretName=cue-secrets \
  --set secretEnv.CUE_API__SECRET_KEY.key=secret-key \
  --set ingress.enabled=true --set ingress.host=cue.example.com
kubectl exec deploy/cue-api -- cuectl keys create admin

env and secretEnv apply to both the API and the worker, so they share the secret key.

  • Configuration: structure (channels, quiet hours) goes in config, which becomes cue.toml in a ConfigMap. Secrets go in secretEnv or envFrom, from your own Secrets.
  • Migrations: every pod runs cuectl db upgrade in an init container. Migrations take a PostgreSQL advisory lock, so replicas starting together wait for each other.
  • Security: pods run as a non-root user with a read-only root filesystem, and drop all capabilities.
  • Tested in CI: the chart is installed on a kind cluster on every change, and the getting-started guide runs against it.

docs.title: Render
docs.text: render.yaml is a Blueprint: New → Blueprint → this repository. It creates the API (migrating on start), a worker and a PostgreSQL database from the published image (a <major>.<minor> tag, which follows patch releases; change it in render.yaml to pin or upgrade), and generates CUE_API__SECRET_KEY for both services. Set CUE_API__PUBLIC_URL when Render asks, then create a key in the API service's shell: cuectl keys create admin.

docs.title: Railway, Heroku and similar platforms
docs.text:
Cue reads the platform's conventions:

  • Database: DATABASE_URL is used when CUE_DATABASE__URL is not set, and plain postgres:// URLs are accepted.
  • Port: cuectl serve listens on PORT when it is set.

On Railway:

  1. Create a project from the image ghcr.io/murtazox04/cue:<version> (or this repository).
  2. Add PostgreSQL, and give the service DATABASE_URL=${{Postgres.DATABASE_URL}}.
  3. Set the start command to cuectl serve --migrate --host 0.0.0.0. Without --host 0.0.0.0 it listens only inside its own container.
  4. Add a second service from the same image with the start command cuectl worker.
  5. If you set CUE_API__PUBLIC_URL, set the same CUE_API__SECRET_KEY on both services.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text: Cue's cost per event is a handful of indexed database statements plus Python work, and it scales by adding worker processes. Measure on your own hardware with the bundled benchmark before sizing a deployment.

docs.title: What one event costs
docs.text:
Step Database statements Transactions Ingest (POST /v1/events) 5: authenticate, find the recipient, insert the event and its job 2 Process the event (rules, policy, render, queue delivery) about 11 3 Deliver (claim, check preferences again, send, record) about 11 3

There are no N+1 patterns: caps, cooldowns, fatigue and agent budgets are each one indexed COUNT (or a LIMIT n read) per message.

docs.title: Run the benchmark
docs.text:
createdb cue_bench
CUE_BENCH_DATABASE_URL=postgresql+asyncpg://localhost/cue_bench \
  uv run python benchmarks/throughput.py --events 20000 --workers 4

The benchmark runs the real application in-process: HTTP through ASGI, the real job queue, the full policy path and template rendering. Delivery goes to a connector that accepts everything instantly, so the numbers measure Cue rather than a provider. Use a throwaway database.

docs.title: Reference numbers
docs.text:
These come from a deliberately modest machine: a 4-vCPU sandboxed cloud container, where every system call is several times slower than on ordinary hardware (a bare SELECT 1 costs about 150 µs). PostgreSQL 16 ran on the same machine. Treat the numbers as a floor; expect more on dedicated hardware.

Setup Ingest (1 API process) Decide and deliver 1 worker process × 16 jobs 146 events/s 56 events/s 4 worker processes × 16 jobs 154 events/s 164 events/s

That is roughly 14 million events a day end to end on 4 vCPUs.

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text:
• Workers scale horizontally. Run one cuectl worker per CPU core, on as many machines as you like. Jobs are claimed with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, so workers never block each other.
  • The API scales the same way: cuectl serve --workers N or more replicas behind a load balancer.
  • Connection pool. Each process keeps worker.concurrency + 4 connections by default, so busy workers do not churn connections. Keep the total across all processes below PostgreSQL's max_connections, or put PgBouncer in front of it.
  • SQLite serialises writes. It suits development and small installations, not high throughput.

docs.title: SDKs
docs.text:
Cue is a plain HTTP API (/openapi.json on any instance generates a client for any language). Two small official clients cover the common cases and, more importantly, verify the signature on webhooks Cue sends to your service.

Language Package Dependencies Source Python 3.10+ cue-notify-client (import cue_client) httpx sdks/python TypeScript / JavaScript cue-client none (Node 18+, Deno, Bun, edge runtimes) sdks/typescript

Both offer the same operations:

Operation Python TypeScript Report an event send_event(name, recipient, data, idempotency_key=) sendEvent({ name, recipient, data, idempotencyKey }) Send a template directly send_message(recipient, template, channels, data, importance=, expires_at=) sendMessage({ … }) Create or update a profile upsert_recipient(id, timezone=, addresses=) upsertRecipient(id, { … }) Read messages get_message(id), list_messages(**filters) getMessage(id), listMessages(filters) Ask a person to approve request_approval(title, reviewers, body, metadata=) requestApproval({ title, reviewers, … }) Read a decision get_approval(id) getApproval(id) Report a bounce or complaint report_feedback(type, channel, address=, provider_message_id=, report_id=) reportFeedback({ type, channel, … }) Verify a webhook verify_webhook(body, header, secret) await verifyWebhook(body, header, secret)

docs.title: Behaviour
docs.text:
• Errors. Error responses raise CueError carrying Cue's problem details: status, title, detail and errors.
  • Retries. HTTP 429, 502, 503 and 504 are retried with backoff (honouring Retry-After), but only for requests that are safe to repeat: reads, profile updates, and sends that carry an idempotency key. A send without a key is never retried, because a retry could notify someone twice.
  • Path safety. Ids are escaped in paths, so a value like ../api-keys cannot reach another endpoint.
  • Async. Python has AsyncCue with the same methods.
  • Agent frameworks. The Python client ships bridges for LangGraph (cue_client.langgraph), Pydantic AI (cue_client.pydantic_ai), CrewAI Flows (cue_client.crewai) and Dapr Agents (cue_client.dapr); none needs the framework installed until it is used.
  • Web frameworks. cue_client.fastapi.CueWebhook (a dependency) and cue_client.django.cue_webhook (a view decorator) check the signature on Cue's webhooks and hand you the parsed payload.
  • Coding agents. The cue-hook command reports OpenHands and Claude Code hook events to Cue; see coding agents. See approval requests.

docs.title: Verifying webhooks
docs.text:
from cue_client import InvalidSignatureError, verify_webhook

try:
    verify_webhook(raw_body, headers.get("Cue-Signature"), WEBHOOK_SECRET)
except InvalidSignatureError:
    ...  # respond 401

Pass the raw body bytes exactly as received. The signature is t=<unix seconds>,v1=<hex HMAC-SHA256 of "<t>.<raw body>">, and requests signed more than five minutes ago are rejected, so a captured request cannot be replayed later. Both SDKs are tested against signatures produced by the server.

docs.title: Quiet hours are harder than they look
docs.text: "Don't send notifications at night" sounds like one if statement. In practice it is a small scheduling problem with three traps: the time a message is decided is not the time it is sent, two different "allowed hours" rules can fight each other, and the clock repeats an hour once a year. This note walks through each one with the concrete bug it produces and the fix Cue ships.

docs.title: 1. Deciding is not sending
docs.text:
The obvious implementation checks quiet hours when the notification is created:

send_at = defer_past_quiet_hours(now, recipient_tz, quiet_hours)
enqueue(message, run_at=send_at)

That is correct for the instant it runs, and wrong for everything that happens after it:

  • Retries. The provider returns a 5xx at 21:55. Exponential backoff schedules the next attempt for 22:40, inside quiet hours that started at 22:00.
  • Slow queues. A broadcast queues 200,000 deliveries at 20:50. The workers drain them over twenty minutes; the tail goes out after 21:00.
  • Human approval. A message from an AI agent waits for a person to approve it. They approve at 23:30, and the "release" code sets send_at = max(send_at, now), which is 23:30.

None of these paths is exotic, and each one sends a message at night that the policy said it would not send. The fix is to treat quiet hours as a property of the send, not of the decision: the delivery worker computes the next allowed moment again right before it calls the provider, and if now is not allowed, it puts the job back with that moment as its run time. Releasing an approved message goes through the same function. Cue has one function, allowed_send_time, used by composing, delivering and releasing, so the three can't drift apart.

docs.title: 2. Two windows that move each other
docs.text:
Marketing text messages in the US have a legal window on top of the user's own quiet hours. Federal rules (47 CFR 64.1200(c)(1)) allow them between 8 a.m. and 9 p.m. at the recipient's location, and several states are narrower; Florida, for example, is 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. with at most three marketing texts a day.

Applying the two rules one after the other looks fine until they interact. Take quiet hours of 21:30–10:00 and a Florida recipient at 21:15:

  1. Quiet hours don't apply yet (21:15 is before 21:30), so the time stays 21:15.
  2. The legal window is closed after 20:00, so the time moves to 08:00 the next day.
  3. 08:00 is inside the user's quiet hours, but nothing checks again.

The message goes out at 08:00, two hours before the person asked to be disturbed. The fix is to apply both constraints in a loop until neither moves the time:

for _ in range(SEND_TIME_ROUNDS):
    moved = defer_past_quiet_hours(when, tz, quiet)
    if window is not None:
        moved = next_allowed(moved, tz, window)
    if moved == when:
        return when
    when = moved

The loop is bounded because some combinations never overlap (quiet hours that cover the whole legal window). In that case the legal window wins: the message goes out at the earliest legal moment rather than never.

docs.title: 3. The hour that happens twice
docs.text:
On the night clocks go back, 02:00–03:00 happens twice in Europe/Berlin. Python's aware datetime objects that share the same ZoneInfo compare by wall-clock time and ignore fold, the attribute that says which of the two 02:30s you mean:

tz = ZoneInfo("Europe/Berlin")
first = datetime(2026, 10, 25, 2, 30, tzinfo=tz, fold=0)
second = datetime(2026, 10, 25, 2, 15, tzinfo=tz, fold=1)

first > second  # True  (wall clock)
first.astimezone(UTC) > second.astimezone(UTC)  # False (00:30 vs 01:15 UTC)

So "is the next 02:30 digest time still ahead of now?" answers yes during the second pass of that hour, even though that 02:30 already happened 45 minutes earlier. A daily digest scheduled that way closes in the past and goes out immediately with a single item; quiet hours that end inside the repeated hour can resume before the message was due. The fix is boring and total: convert both sides to UTC before comparing, everywhere a local schedule is compared with now.

docs.title: 4. Waiting is not the same as being throttled
docs.text:
Once the delivery worker can say "not now, try at 07:00", it needs a way to put the job back. A job queue usually already has one: the "retry later" path used for provider rate limits. That path has sensible guards for throttling, such as capping each delay at an hour and giving up after a day of deferrals, so one flaky provider can't hold a job forever.

Those guards are wrong for planned waits. A message held until quiet hours end ten hours from now would wake up every hour, defer again, and burn worker time. Worse, an approval request that expires in a week would be given up on after a day of "deferring". Cue now distinguishes the two: a planned wait keeps its full delay and never counts toward the throttling limits, while a provider's Retry-After still does.

docs.title: 5. Caps count the future too
docs.text: Frequency caps ("at most one marketing message per day") have the same shape of bug. The first implementation counted every message in the category with send_at after now - period, which includes messages scheduled for next week. One reminder planned three days out silently used up today's budget. A cap should count only the messages in a window of period around the candidate send time.

docs.title: The common thread
docs.text:
Every one of these bugs came from treating a time as known when it was decided. Retries, approvals, queues, clock changes and future schedules all move the moment a message actually reaches someone, and the rules have to hold at that moment. In Cue each of these cases has a regression test that sets the clock and checks when the message goes out.

The code is MIT on GitHub; the delivery policy page lists the rules as they work today.

docs.title: HTTP API
docs.text: The complete, always-current reference is generated from the code: open /docs (Swagger UI) or /redoc on a running instance, or fetch /openapi.json to generate a client.

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text:
• Authentication: Authorization: Bearer ck_…. Keys carry scopes.
  • Errors use RFC 9457 problem details (application/problem+json) with title, status, detail and, for validation errors, an errors list. See problem responses.
  • Pagination: list endpoints take limit (≤ 500) and cursor, and return {"items": [...], "next_cursor": "…" | null}. Results are newest first.
  • Idempotency: events take idempotency_key; direct sends take idempotency_key. A repeat returns 200 with the original resource instead of 202.
  • Timestamps are ISO 8601 in UTC.
  • Statuses and reasons of messages, events, digests, broadcasts and approval requests are listed in statuses and reasons.

docs.title: Endpoints
docs.text:
Method & path Scope POST /v1/events events:write Ingest an event. Inline region, attributes, addresses, or a changed locale/timezone, also need recipients:write. GET /v1/events, GET /v1/events/{id} messages:read Events with per-rule outcomes. POST /v1/messages messages:write Send a template directly. GET /v1/messages, GET /v1/messages/{id} messages:read Filter by recipient, status, event_id, broadcast_id, agent. POST /v1/messages/{id}/approve, …/reject approvals:decide Review a message an agent sent that is pending_approval. POST /v1/messages/{id}/cancel messages:write Cancel a queued message. POST /v1/messages/{id}/engagement events:write Record delivered/opened/clicked/converted. POST /v1/track/{tracking_token} none (the token) Engagement from client apps. POST /v1/approvals messages:write Ask people to approve an action. GET /v1/approvals, GET /v1/approvals/{id} messages:read Approval requests and their decisions. POST /v1/approvals/{id}/approve, …/reject approvals:decide Decide an approval request. GET /v1/digests, GET /v1/digests/{id} messages:read Grouped events; filter by recipient, status. POST /v1/digests/{id}/send messages:write Close a digest's window early. PUT /v1/recipients/{external_id} recipients:write Create or update. GET /v1/recipients, GET /v1/recipients/{external_id} recipients:read DELETE /v1/recipients/{external_id} recipients:write Erase profile and history. POST /v1/recipients/{id}/addresses recipients:write Add a device, number, e-mail…; re-enables a disabled address. DELETE /v1/recipients/{id}/addresses/{channel}/{value} recipients:write PUT /v1/recipients/{id}/preferences recipients:write Unsubscribes, muted channels, quiet hours. POST /v1/recipients/{id}/consent recipients:write Record an opt-in with its disclosure; see compliance. GET /v1/recipients/{id}/preferences/history recipients:read Consent ledger. POST /v1/recipients/{id}/preference-token recipients:write Rotate the preference token. GET, PUT /v1/preferences/{token} none (the token) Self-service preferences for your own UI. POST /v1/inbound/sms recipients:write STOP/START replies from any SMS provider (not for agent keys). POST /v1/inbound/twilio none (Twilio signature) Twilio's incoming-message webhook; needs api.public_url. POST /v1/inbound/twilio/status none (Twilio signature) Twilio's delivery status callback: delivery feedback. POST /v1/inbound/resend/{channel} none (Svix signature) Resend's webhook for a resend channel: delivery feedback. POST /v1/inbound/ses/{channel} none (SNS signature, listed topics) Amazon SNS notifications for an ses channel: delivery feedback. POST /v1/feedback recipients:write Report a delivery, bounce, soft bounce or spam complaint (not for agent keys). /v1/templates[/{key}], POST …/{key}/preview admin /v1/rules[/{key}], POST /v1/rules/evaluate admin /v1/categories[/{key}] admin /v1/broadcasts[/{id}], …/start, …/pause, …/resume, …/cancel admin /v1/agents[/{key}] admin Automated senders: budgets, importance ceiling, approval. /v1/api-keys, …/{id}/revoke admin Keys may be bound to an agent. GET, POST /preferences/{token} none (the token) Hosted preference page. GET, POST /preferences/{token}/unsubscribe none (the token) Confirmation page and RFC 8058 one-click unsubscribe. GET, POST /review/{token} none (the token) One-time review page for a held message or approval request. GET /healthz, GET /readyz none Liveness and readiness (checks the database). GET /metrics none Prometheus metrics, only with metrics = true; keep it off public ingress. GET /docs, /redoc, /openapi.json none Interactive docs and the OpenAPI schema, unless api.docs = false.

The routes without a key are rate limited per client address; see api.rate_limit.

docs.title: Messages
docs.text:
Direct sends are for messages your code decides to send — one-time codes, receipts, alerts:

POST /v1/messages
{
  "recipient": "user-42",
  "template": "login-code",
  "category": "transactional",
  "channels": ["sms"],
  "data": {"code": "482913"},
  "idempotency_key": "login-7f3a"
}

They pass the same policy as everything else; check the returned status.

docs.title: CLI
docs.text:
cuectl serve [--host 127.0.0.1] [--port 8000] [--workers 1] [--reload] [--migrate]
cuectl worker [--concurrency N] [--once]
cuectl mcp [--url URL] [--transport stdio|streamable-http] [--host 127.0.0.1] [--port 8765]
                                   MCP server for AI agents (see guides/ai-agents);
                                   key from CUE_API_KEY, HTTP token from CUE_MCP_AUTH_TOKEN
cuectl check                      validate configuration and database connectivity;
                                  exits 1 on unsafe settings (listed under "warnings")
cuectl db upgrade [REVISION]      apply migrations (default: head)
cuectl db downgrade REVISION
cuectl db current
cuectl keys create NAME [-s SCOPE]... [--agent AGENT]
                                  print a new API key once, optionally bound to an
                                  agent; without -s: admin, or with --agent:
                                  events:write, messages:write, messages:read
cuectl keys list
cuectl keys revoke KEY_ID
cuectl jobs stats                 queued and dead jobs by kind
cuectl jobs retry-dead [--kind K]
                                  requeue dead jobs and reopen the events, messages,
                                  broadcasts and digests they gave up on
cuectl prune [--older-than DAYS] [--ledger-older-than DAYS] [--batch-size N]
                                  delete old events, finished messages, closed digests,
                                  decided approval requests, expired review links,
                                  dead jobs and the ids of applied delivery reports;
                                  the consent ledger only when asked.
                                  Deletes N rows (1000) per transaction
cuectl version                    (or cuectl --version)

serve binds to 127.0.0.1; pass --host 0.0.0.0 to listen on every interface (the container image, Compose file, Helm chart and Render Blueprint do).

keys create without -s gives the key admin. With --agent it gives the key every scope an agent key may hold instead: events:write, messages:write and messages:read. Pass -s to narrow it further, for example cuectl keys create helper-key --agent helper -s events:write -s messages:read. Agent keys cannot hold admin, recipients:read, recipients:write or approvals:decide; asking for one of them fails. See API key scopes.

worker --once processes every job that is due and exits — useful for cron-style deployments and debugging. All commands read the same configuration.

prune does not run by itself: schedule it (cron, a Kubernetes CronJob, your platform's scheduler), for example daily. See deployment.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Settings are read, highest precedence first, from:

  1. environment variables — prefix CUE_, nested keys joined with __ (CUE_DATABASE__URL, CUE_CHANNELS__SMS__AUTH_TOKEN);
  2. a .env file in the working directory;
  3. a TOML file: ./cue.toml, or the path in CUE_CONFIG_FILE (which must exist).

A complete example lives in examples/cue.toml. Run cuectl check to validate a configuration.

docs.title: Top level
docs.text: Key Default environment development development, test or production. log_level INFO log_format console json for log shippers (the Docker image defaults to json). metrics false Expose Prometheus metrics at /metrics (needs the metrics extra).

docs.title: database
docs.text: Key Default url sqlite+aiosqlite:///./cue.db Use postgresql+asyncpg://user:pass@host/db in production. pool_size / max_overflow worker concurrency + 4 / 10 Per process (PostgreSQL). echo false Log SQL.

docs.title: api
docs.text:
Key Default cors_origins [] Origins allowed to call the API from a browser. docs true Serve /docs, /redoc and /openapi.json. root_path "" When mounted under a path prefix behind a proxy. public_url none Public base URL (with any path prefix). Enables preference and unsubscribe links. Requires secret_key. secret_key none Signs preference tokens, so the database never holds a working link. At least 32 characters; required with public_url. Set it as CUE_API__SECRET_KEY. See below. product_name none Shown on the hosted preference page. max_body_bytes 1048576 Larger request bodies get 413 before anything reads them. max_broadcast_body_bytes 67108864 The same limit for POST /v1/broadcasts with an admin key, whose audience can list a million ids. Without one, max_body_bytes applies. trusted_proxies [] Addresses or networks (10.0.0.0/8) of your reverse proxies. Only requests from them have X-Forwarded-For believed when rate limiting.

public_url with plain http:// (other than localhost) logs a warning at startup and fails cuectl check: the links it builds carry tokens.

docs.title: api.secret_key
docs.text:
Generate it once and keep it in your secret store:

python -c 'import secrets; print(secrets.token_urlsafe(32))'
  • Required with public_url. Without it Cue refuses to start. It can be set on its own too: then preference_token and templates' links.token work for your own preference screen, without hosted links.
  • Shared. Give the same value to every API and worker process. A link signed by one process must verify on all the others.
  • Rotation. Changing it invalidates every preference and unsubscribe link signed with the old value, including those in e-mails already delivered. Rotate it only if it leaks; to cut off one person's links, rotate their token instead (POST /v1/recipients/{id}/preference-token).
  • Unset. Without it, preference_token and links.token are null and messages carry no preference or unsubscribe links.

docs.title: api.rate_limit
docs.text:
Per client address, in each process. Requests over a limit get 429 with Retry-After.

Key Default enabled true pages {per_minute = 60, burst = 30} /preferences/…, /review/… and /v1/preferences/…. tracking {per_minute = 600, burst = 300} /v1/track/…. inbound {per_minute = 600, burst = 300} /v1/inbound/…, except status callbacks. feedback {per_minute = 6000, burst = 3000} Delivery status callbacks and provider webhooks: /v1/inbound/twilio/status, /v1/inbound/resend/…, /v1/inbound/ses/…. failed_auth {per_minute = 10, burst = 20} Responses 401 on /v1; once used up, requests from that address without a valid key get 429 on /v1 until it refills. Valid keys are never blocked by it. max_clients 100000 Addresses remembered; the least recently seen are forgotten first.

docs.title: delivery
docs.text:
Delivery feedback and channel health.

Key Default soft_bounce_limit 3 Soft bounces in a row (no delivery between) that disable an address. breaker_failures 5 Transient failures in a row after which a channel is skipped when another is planned. 0 turns this off. breaker_cooldown_seconds 60 How long a failing channel is skipped. Then one message at a time tries it: a success closes the breaker, a failure skips it for another cooldown.

docs.title: worker
docs.text: Key Default embedded false Run the worker inside the API process. concurrency 16 Concurrent jobs per worker process. poll_interval 1.0 Seconds between polls when idle. lease_seconds 300 How long a claimed job is hidden from other workers. max_attempts 10 Attempts before a job is marked dead. A job whose worker died this many times is marked dead when it is next claimed. retry_base_seconds / retry_max_seconds 5 / 3600 Exponential backoff with jitter. shutdown_timeout 30 Seconds to finish in-flight jobs on shutdown; jobs still running are cancelled and handed back at once. job_timeout 120 Seconds a job may run before it is cancelled; a timeout is retried like any other failure. max_defer_seconds 86400 How long a job may keep deferring (rate limits, Retry-After) before it is marked dead. Deferrals do not count towards max_attempts.

docs.title: policy
docs.text: Key Default default_locale en For recipients without a locale. default_timezone UTC For recipients without a valid time zone. quiet_hours {start = "22:00", end = "08:00"} null disables the default window.

docs.title: channels.<name>
docs.text: provider selects the implementation; enabled = false turns a channel off. Every other key belongs to the provider — see Channels. Names are lowercase letters, digits, - and _.

docs.title: ai
docs.text: Key Default enabled false model — Pydantic AI model id (provider:model). Required when enabled. fallback_models [] Tried in order if the primary fails. instructions — Brand voice for every message. temperature 0.7 max_output_tokens 512 timeout 20 Seconds per request. daily_token_budget — Tokens per UTC day; afterwards template text is used.

docs.title: screening
docs.text:
Screens agents' messages before delivery.

Key Default enabled false provider typesafe TypeSafe's Jev decision model. api_key TYPESAFE_API_KEY Required when enabled. base_url https://api.typesafe.ai model jev-latest timeout 5 Seconds per request. hold_above 0.5 Hold a message when any risk is at least this likely. min_confidence 0.6 Lower importance only when the urgency answer is this sure. on_error hold hold or send a message when screening fails.

docs.title: approvals
docs.text:
Where decisions on approval requests are reported.

Key Default callback_url — Receives a signed POST for each decision. callback_secret — Signs callbacks (Cue-Signature). Required with callback_url. timeout 10 Seconds per callback request. max_pending_per_agent 10 Open requests one agent may have; more get 429. Requests from keys not bound to an agent are not limited.

docs.title: compliance
docs.text:
Legal safety nets for marketing text messages; see Compliance.

Key Default us_texting_rules false Hold marketing texts to US legal hours and state caps. sms_channels ["sms"] Channels that send text messages. unknown_state strict Rules for US recipients without a region: strict or federal.

docs.title: API key scopes
docs.text:
Every API key carries one or more scopes. admin implies all the others. Create keys with cuectl keys create NAME -s SCOPE… or POST /v1/api-keys, and give each caller only what it needs.

Scope Allows events:write POST /v1/events; POST /v1/messages/{id}/engagement. Inline recipient profiles may create a recipient, fill an empty locale or timezone, or repeat the stored values. messages:write POST /v1/messages (direct sends), POST /v1/messages/{id}/cancel, POST /v1/digests/{id}/send, POST /v1/approvals (ask people to approve an action). messages:read GET /v1/messages[/{id}], GET /v1/events[/{id}], GET /v1/digests[/{id}], GET /v1/approvals[/{id}]. recipients:write Create, update and erase recipients, add and remove addresses, replace preferences, record consent, rotate preference tokens, POST /v1/inbound/sms. Also needed to set region, attributes or addresses inline on an event or send, or to change a stored locale or timezone that way. recipients:read GET /v1/recipients[/{id}] (including preference_token) and the consent ledger. approvals:decide Approve or reject held messages (POST /v1/messages/{id}/approve, /reject) and approval requests (POST /v1/approvals/{id}/approve, /reject). Give it to the keys your people decide with, not to the keys that send. admin Everything above, plus templates, rules (including the /v1/rules/evaluate dry run), categories, broadcasts, agents and API keys. Only admin keys may send broadcast bodies up to api.max_broadcast_body_bytes and see review links in message content; other keys see /review/[redacted].

A key without the scope a route needs gets 403. The routes that need no key are listed in the HTTP API reference.

docs.title: Typical keys
docs.text:
cuectl keys create setup                                   # admin, for the operator
cuectl keys create backend -s events:write -s messages:write -s messages:read \
  -s recipients:write                                      # your application
cuectl keys create approvals-ui -s approvals:decide -s messages:read
cuectl keys create dashboard -s messages:read -s recipients:read

docs.title: Keys bound to an agent
docs.text:
A key created with --agent acts for an agent: its budget, importance ceiling, categories and approval policy apply to everything it sends.

  • It can hold only events:write, messages:write and messages:read. Asking for admin, recipients:read, recipients:write or approvals:decide is refused with 422, and an older key that holds one of them is denied it on every request.
  • cuectl keys create NAME --agent X without -s gives it those three scopes; narrow them with -s, for example -s events:write -s messages:read for an agent that only reports events.
  • It refers to people by external id only: inline profiles are refused with 403.
  • It sees only the messages and events it sent, and no digests.
  • Its events always have the source agent:<key>; the cue.* event names and the source cue are reserved.
  • It cannot cancel or report engagement on other senders' messages, report SMS replies, or change anyone's preferences.
  • Keys of a disabled agent are refused on every endpoint.

docs.title: Statuses and reasons
docs.text: Every decision Cue makes is stored. This page lists the values you will find in status, status_reason and an event's outcome, and the error responses of the API.

docs.title: Message status
docs.text:
GET /v1/messages/{id} → status.

Status Meaning Final queued Accepted and waiting for its send time. Can still be cancelled. no sending Claimed by a worker and being handed to a provider; can no longer be cancelled. no pending_approval Held until a person approves it (agent approval policy or screening). Not sent. no sent A provider accepted it. yes delivered The provider or the client app confirmed delivery. yes failed Every planned channel failed permanently, retries ran out, or the template could not be rendered. yes suppressed Policy decided against sending it; see status_reason. yes cancelled Withdrawn before sending: cancelled through the API, its broadcast was cancelled, or a reviewer rejected it. yes

Engagement (opened, clicked, converted) is tracked separately from the status; see engagement tracking.

docs.title: Message status_reason
docs.text:
Policy reasons come first in the order Cue checks them. Some carry detail after a colon.

status_reason Status Why duplicate suppressed The same event and rule, broadcast and recipient, or send idempotency_key already produced a message. Only seen in dry runs: a real duplicate returns the original message. unsubscribed suppressed The person left this category. Checked again right before sending. consent_expired suppressed The opt-in recorded for this category has expired. no_reachable_channel suppressed or failed When composing (suppressed): the person has no enabled address on any of the planned channels (or muted them), or none of those channels is configured. At send time (failed): no address was left to try. compliance: <cap> marketing texts per 24 hours (<source>) suppressed US state texting cap, with [compliance] us_texting_rules. See compliance. cooldown suppressed The rule already sent to this person within cooldown_seconds. expired suppressed The message could not go out before expires_at: quiet hours or texting hours pushed it past its expiry, it waited for approval too long, or it was still queued when it expired. frequency_cap: <limit> per <period> suppressed The category's rolling cap is used up around the send time, e.g. frequency_cap: 3 per 1 day, 0:00:00. fatigue suppressed The person ignored this category's recent messages; see policy. agent_budget: <limit> per <period> suppressed The sending agent used its attention budget for this person. agent_not_allowed suppressed Checked right before sending: the sending agent was disabled, or may no longer use the message's category. agent_deleted suppressed Checked right before sending: the sending agent was deleted. template_error: <detail> failed The template has no usable locale or failed to render. screening: <risks> pending_approval Screening held it: pressure, deception, secret, critical not confirmed, or screening unavailable when the screening API failed and on_error = "hold". rejected or rejected: <reason> cancelled A reviewer rejected it. cancelled via API cancelled POST /v1/messages/{id}/cancel. broadcast cancelled cancelled Its broadcast was cancelled. gave up: <error> failed Its delivery job used up worker.max_attempts (or max_defer_seconds). cuectl jobs retry-dead reopens it. provider errors, joined by ; failed Every channel failed permanently; one entry per channel. null any Nothing to explain: queued, sent, delivered, or approved and queued.

docs.title: Event status and rule outcomes
docs.text:
GET /v1/events/{id} → status is pending (waiting for the worker), processed, or failed (processing gave up; the reason is in error).

outcome has one entry per rule whose event pattern matched the name:

reason matched Meaning outside_rollout false The recipient is not in the rule's rollout_percent. condition_false false The rule's condition did not hold. condition_error: <detail> false The condition could not be evaluated for this event. misconfigured true The rule's template or category is missing. agent_not_allowed true The event came from an agent that may not use the rule's category, or the agent is disabled. agent_deleted true The event came from an agent that was deleted before the event was processed. digested true The event joined a digest (digest_id). a message reason true A message was composed: status and message_id are set, and reason is the message's status_reason above (absent when it is null).

Rules lower in priority than a matching rule with stop_processing are not listed. Wildcard rules (*, cue.*) never see Cue's own cue.* events.

docs.title: Other statuses
docs.text: Resource Values Digest open (collecting until closes_at), sent (composed into a message, which policy may still suppress), cancelled (discarded, e.g. its rule was disabled). Broadcast draft, scheduled, running, paused, completed, cancelled, failed. Approval request pending, approved, rejected, expired (nobody decided before expires_at; treat it as a no). A request past its expires_at reads as expired even before the expiry job has run. Consent ledger source api, self_service, one_click, sms_keyword.

docs.title: Problem responses
docs.text:
Errors are RFC 9457 problem details (application/problem+json): {"type": "about:blank", "title", "status", "detail"}, plus errors (each with loc, msg, type) for validation errors.

Status Title When 400 Bad request A request the service cannot act on. 401 Unauthorized No API key, or an unknown, revoked or expired one (WWW-Authenticate: Bearer). 403 Forbidden The key lacks the scope; an agent key reaching past its limits (other categories, other senders' messages, recipient profiles, reserved cue.* names); a disabled agent; changing a stored profile inline without recipients:write; an invalid Twilio signature. 404 Not found The resource, or the preference page for a token, does not exist. 409 Conflict Duplicate keys, concurrent changes (retry), or an action the resource's state does not allow (title Invalid state), such as approving a message that is not waiting. 410 Gone A review link or approval link that was already used or has expired. 413 Content too large The body is over api.max_body_bytes (or max_broadcast_body_bytes). 422 Unprocessable content Validation failed, or a request that cannot be honoured, such as an agent key with a forbidden scope. 429 Too many requests A rate limit (with Retry-After), or an agent over approvals.max_pending_per_agent. 500 Internal server error Logged with the request path.

The hosted preference and review pages show the same errors as HTML pages.
